leads.title: Bounty program: community detection/DLP rules with corpus fixtures
leads.description:
# Detection rule bounty program

Agentmetry's detection engine is only as good as its rules. This program turns the
open `detection-rule` / `dlp-rule` issues (tagged `bounty`) into a community
contribution track with a defined bar, so anyone can ship a rule and have it
counted in CI forever.

## What counts as a bounty contribution

A new detection or DLP rule that ships with:

1. The rule registered in `apps/orchestrator/agentmetry/core/audit/detection/` (or a YAML rule where that is the right surface).
2. **Corpus fixtures**: at least one `attack_*.jsonl` session in `corpus/` that must fire the rule, plus a `benign_*.jsonl` session that must stay silent. Expectations go in `corpus.yaml` and are written from what the session *is*, not from what the engine currently prints.
3. A Sigma export where the rule is expressible as Sigma (the engine already generates these; keep it working).
4. ATT&CK / ATLAS tags where applicable, and a one-paragraph note in the rule docstring citing the incident or pattern it models.

The gate is `agentmetry benchmark` plus the full test suite: the README "Checked claims" numbers update automatically via `test_readme_claims.py`, so your PR must include the refreshed README block.

## Rewards

- **Recognition**: listed in `CONTRIBUTORS.md`, a "certified rule" mention in the release notes, and the rule named in the docs.
- **Priority review**: bounty PRs get a maintainer review within 7 days; the corpus gate makes review mechanical.
- **Cash (when funded)**: NLnet NGI and similar grants earmark bounties for exactly this kind of contribution; when a funding round lands, tagged `bounty` issues get paid bounties (amount announced per round in Discussions). Until then the reward is recognition + fast review.

## How to claim

Comment "claim" on a `bounty`-tagged issue (or open a new one describing the attack
pattern). One rule per PR. If you are new to the repo, start with a `good first issue` instead.

## Not in scope

- Enterprise-only features (those live in the private repo).
- Rules that require weakening the privacy minimization (no full paths/argv/usernames in the trail).
- Changes that make existing corpus cases fail; if a rule legitimately re-labels an existing case, say so explicitly in the PR.

leads.title: Show HN: Bot-bottle – secure runtime, DLP and remote control for local agents
leads.description: Hey! About 6 months ago, I started looking for a tool to safely run coding agents on my (security sensitive) developer machine. Specifically, I wanted a tool that: - I could use regardless of the model or harness running underneath - I could build simple, composable, plaintext security policies for - Provided strong vm level isolation - Hid credentials from agents - Scanned and monitored everything going in and out of agent workspace - Allowed me to use the same mobile flow I had gotten used to with claude code, but with arbitrary harnesses I couldn't find a tool that met all of these, so I started bot-bottle. It's evolved into what I'm hoping will be the best security conscious, local first coding agent orchestrator out there. Here's how it works: Each agent runs in its own microVM (Firecracker on Linux, Apple's container on macOS, Docker as a weaker fallback), with whichever harness you want. Claude Code, Codex and pi are built in, and custom agent providers are supported (still being documented/tested). What an agent can reach is defined in a "bottle", which is just a short markdown file listing hosts, repos and which secret goes to which host. Bottles are enforced by a gateway outside the agent VM, which adds the real credentials to requests on the way out, so the agent only sees placeholders. Bottles stack, so you can keep small ones around (npm read only, one repo, one API, etc) and combine them per task. Repos can ship their own bottles, which only run after you trust their exact contents. Outgoing requests and git pushes are scanned for secrets, and everything is logged locally (you can stream it to your own endpoint as NDJSON or OCSF). Anything a bottle doesn't allow comes to you for approval, in the terminal or on your phone through an optional paired console. It's in alpha (the console especially), so UI polish is still in progress. Install: curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/diderisoft/bot-bottle/main/install.sh | sh Docs: https://bot-bottle.com/docs Would love feedback, especially on the threat model and on whether bottles are the right abstraction.

leads.title: Show HN: Mimzie, an agent-neutral alternative to the Claude Suite/Claude Cowork
leads.description: hi HN! I built Mimzie, an agent neutral AI workspace inspired by the Claude Suite (Docs, Sheets, Slides) and Cowork. It's a free desktop app that runs ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and Grok in their native CLI harnesses. Think T3 Code or Conductor but for knowledge work. It's basically a GUI for managing knowledge work agents in various form factors. One of those form factors is Bots, akin to Grok Bot or Dots. The original idea for mimzie was simple: I pay for Claude and ChatGPT, and a lot of my day-to-day work lives in .xlsx, .pptx and .docx files. Moreover, I was sick and tired of losing context between AI platforms. I didn't want to bet the house on one AI lab's product, be it the ChatGPT or the Claude Desktop app. So I built an AI desktop app that was agent neutral. The goal of mimzie is to bring the kind of agent workflows that devs have had with codex and claude code into the hands of everyone. And to have a friendly GUI to do it. I've found that the personal agents, hermes and openclaw, are intimidating to set up and confusing to the average non-technical person. some of the core principles of mimzie: - your file stays your file: edits are done locally and .docx, .pptx, .xlsx, and .md and synced to the cloud after - every change is reviewable: edits show up as tracked diffs that you accept or reject, at the smallest unit that makes sense (e.g. a sentence in .docx) - free, and no new subscription needed: bring whichever AI plan or plans you already have. You shouldn't have to pay twice for the same inference, and you SHOULD take advantage of the insane subsidization in the current ChatGPT and Claude plans. - Bots with any AI: I love the concept of grok bot, not so much its limited choice of models. I strongly believe that long-standing "ai teammates" should be agent neutral and in your control Try mimzie out: it's a free beta at mimzie.com it's early, lots of rough edges, but I've had the time of my life developing it. I'd love to answer questions and hear any and all feedback.

leads.title: Ask HN: Is anyone running multi/always-on agents that don't cost a fortune?
leads.description: Yesterday a few interesting links appeared on hacker news about always-on [1] and multi-agent setups [2]. Some of those points resonate with what we're experiencing with our current approach of running agents and sub-agents locally. - We are delegating complex and long running tasks to agents more and more. Being able to run those overnight seems like a logical next step in efficiency, because at the moment we are stopping the local agents every evening and restarting them in the morning. - A setup with decentralized multi-agent system with shared context is 5.5x faster than Claude code + native subagents. It takes 29.3 minutes (2% of agent time waiting) versus 162.7 minutes (44% of agent time waiting). [3] This aligns with our feeling that locally running agents are often "doing nothing" while waiting on test results, each other, and so on - The possibility to monitor "input channels" (e.g. chat channels, e-mail inboxes...) and have agents act autonomously on those seems like something that could help us out as well. This all sounds amazing, but we're unsure how others are currently doing this and what those cost. We currently mainly power our needs via subscription-based contracts (e.g. claude (code) pro/max, chatgpt plus/pro ...) - Is anyone running such multi-agent or always-on agent systems? - Do you host it yourself, or do you use existings solutions like grok bots or claude remote control sessions or claude routines? - Can you make this work with subscriptions, or do you use API pricing, or even self-hosted LLMs? How do the costs compare with running local agents? - How are the results? Is it an improvement? [1] Stanford CS146S: How always-on agents work Lecture: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=L1OBRtfPS34 Slides: https://drive.google.com/file/d/1b8WiBk_lcB3ue-jZMLijSUMLj6SDiF6Z/view [2] CMU 11-768 AI Agents: https://www.cmu-agents.com/#/schedule [3] Decentralized Multi-Agent Systems with Shared Context (figure 3, page 3): https://arxiv.org/pdf/2606.10662

leads.title: Show HN: Pi-maestro – spec driven development for Pi
leads.description: https://github.com/emilioSp/pi-maestro Pi Maestro started from my need to use an engineering method when working with agents. With simple prompts or the "let’s write a plan" approach, I would sometimes reach dead ends and have to start over. Agents would say the work was complete too early, without checking the result enough. Spec-driven development seemed suitable for this problem. So I tried to turn it into a workflow that worked in practice: define the expected behavior, ask one agent to implement it, and ask another to check it independently. At first, I tried to do everything through skills. However, I noticed that agents would skip steps in the protocol described in the Markdown files. My impression was that following the workflow required too much attention compared to the assigned task. So I introduced deterministic tools that control transitions and check the reports produced by agents. Basically, I built a finite state machine where each step requires a structured handoff. This handoff also becomes the starting point for the next agent. Taking inspiration from OpenSpec and GitHub Spec Kit, I adopted the concepts that suited the way I work: proposal.md for the context, goal, and scope of the change. spec.md for requirements in the form "actor MUST…" and acceptance criteria using GIVEN, WHEN, THEN and concrete examples. design.md when important technical decisions are needed. Once the spec is written and approved, the Maestro (orchestrator) starts coordinating a sequence of agents: Builder, responsible for implementation. Verifier, responsible for checking that everything works as specified. Simplifier, responsible for simplifying the code to make it clearer. I have chosen Pi because it provides events to control the runtime. This made it easy to add the maestro without going through an MCP server. Pi also works with different LLM models. Using different models for each role allows for a more critical view of the spec: a builder and a verifier from the same "family" will approach the problem in similar ways. I'd like to have your feedback on it and in general on the spec-driven development. Do you use spec-driven development? If Yes, which workflow best suit for your needs?

leads.title: [bounty] bug-report: 'import collections' resolves to Python builtins module, not stdlib/collections.ltl
leads.description:
Claiming the recurring $10 bug-report bounty.

## Minimal reproducer

```lateralus
import collections
fn main() -> int {
    let s = collections.Stack();
    return 0;
}
```

On main (621ae1b): `AttributeError: module 'builtins' has no attribute 'Stack'`
— `import collections` binds the name to Python's builtins `collections`
module, not `stdlib/collections.ltl`.

`import math` and `import algorithms` correctly resolve to the .ltl
stdlib modules (math.sqrt / algorithms.gcd verified working), so the
stdlib search path works — `collections` specifically collides with a
Python module name.

## Why it's a bug

Spec §15.3 documents `collections.Stack`, `Queue`, `Deque`,
`PriorityQueue`, `TreeSet`, `HashMap`, `LinkedList`, `CircularBuffer`
as stdlib collections. `stdlib/collections.ltl` exists in the repo —
the import system should prefer it over (or namespace it away from)
Python's same-named module.

## Fix sketch

Import resolution: prefer stdlib/*.ltl over Python builtins when a
name matches both (or emit a distinct module object so stdlib attrs
win). Check how math/algorithms resolve vs collections.

leads.title: Full sovereignty and network exit test
leads.description:
The final integration challenge: a reproducible environment where independent community operators run the entire decentralized protocol without a Hanzo-controlled control plane, exercising peer discovery, model retrieval, job scheduling, inference, verification, payment, state recovery and governance. References: Zoo network-architecture paper, libp2p.

Acceptance: deliberately disable Hanzo-operated gateways, registries, schedulers and infrastructure; a separately administered network still accepts new providers, discovers models, executes and verifies a request, settles payment and recovers the user's authorized data. A network that requires api.hanzo.ai to stay online is not decentralized at the protocol level.

Part of the fully decentralized Hanzo program (tracking issue in hanzoai/cloud). Rules for every bounty: (1) do not build another isolated AI stack: reuse Hanzo's engine, Enso routing, Visor, VFS and API protocols and extend them through versioned interfaces; (2) no mandatory Hanzo-controlled dependency: Hanzo-operated services may be conveniences but every critical function needs an independently operable protocol path; (3) open source and defensible proof claims: prefer Apache-2.0/MIT, check model and dataset licenses independently, and never conflate cryptographic proofs, hardware attestations and economically incentivized verification. Measure on every bounty: cost (dollars per million useful tokens including verification and settlement), performance (TTFT, throughput, tail latency, completion rate), trust (share of incorrect or fraudulent work detected under the declared threat model), decentralization (share of work that proceeds without Hanzo-operated infrastructure) and sovereignty (users and providers can export, migrate, operate or fork their services and data). Security-critical contracts and verification protocols need external review before they hold real funds. Open for community research: comment to claim, publish method and raw numbers (bounty; reward terms are set by the maintainers on the issue).

leads.title: [bounty] bug-report: Python correlation returns zero for identical nonconstant vectors at small scale
leads.description:
Lateralus 3.2.0 (`ed5b9eabd18f4ebdb0eaa8c765b7812f7c393ca3`), Python 3.12.14, Linux x86_64. Codex was used to inspect the generated Python runtime and run this reproduction.

Save as `correlation.ltl` and run `PYTHONPATH=. python -m lateralus_lang run correlation.ltl` from the checkout.

```text
println(correlation([0.0, 0.00000000000001], [0.0, 0.00000000000001]))
println(correlation([0.0, 1.0], [0.0, 1.0]))
```

Actual output is `0.0` followed by `1.0`. Both pairs contain identical, nonconstant vectors, so Pearson correlation is 1 in both cases. Scaling both vectors changes the result.

The Python emitter's built-in `correlation` returns zero whenever either standard deviation is below `1e-12`. Here each standard deviation is `5e-15` and the covariance is `2.5e-29`, so the denominator is nonzero. A regression test could compare these two scales while preserving the existing zero-variance behavior.

```python
def correlation(xs,ys):
    sx,sy=std_dev(xs),std_dev(ys)
    return 0.0 if sx<1e-12 or sy<1e-12 else covariance(xs,ys)/(sx*sy)
```

Source: [`lateralus_lang/codegen/python.py`](https://github.com/bad-antics/lateralus-lang/blob/ed5b9eabd18f4ebdb0eaa8c765b7812f7c393ca3/lateralus_lang/codegen/python.py) at that commit (the `correlation` builtin emitted into the runtime).

Duplicate search just before filing: no open or closed issue or pull request mentions this `correlation` cutoff, Pearson correlation, or these inputs. [#186](https://github.com/bad-antics/lateralus-lang/issues/186) is a different absolute-threshold bug (`Matrix.det` / `inverse` at `1e-15`). No patch is attached.

I'm submitting this under the advertised $10 minimal-reproducer bounty in `BOUNTIES.md`. Could you confirm the claim and whether you want a separate patch?

leads.description: Hello, I’m Oscar. I’ve been leading dev teams from Barcelona with my cofounder Uri for a long time. We pushed the use of AI a lot, allowing an increase in the code shipment velocity, but our job as seniors moved from building to just reviewing. We also started to see a lot of drift in how devs were doing the code, less standards, less control, which caused more bugs and differences between what product department asked and what we shipped. It was impossible for us to keep reviewing everything by hand, so we decided to clone how we review as humans into a product: Revix AI. In easy words, Revix main strength is that it extracts from your repo all the good practices and team standards, then on every pull request comments if anything moves from that. That, paired with PR status badges and targeted notifications allowed us to reduce review time by 54% on many teams, while increasing the confidence and reducing bugs on production. We know there are other similar products around and they work fine, but we found that they trust too much on the LLM and focus just on bug hunting. Our philosophy goes further, we created a system that reviews the same as a senior engineer would do, not catching just bugs. We achieved to comment only on things devs actually fix and stop the noise. Revix AI works on GitHub, Gitlab, Bitbucket and can sync with many other tools like Slack, Jira, Linear etc. Please feel free to request any other tool that we still do not support. We offer free reviews for any open source project, and for companies we do price per seat including a 14 days free trial. leads.title: Show HN: TrnRT – An open-source LLM inference engine for AWS Trainium
leads.description: Hi HN, Sanchit here from RunAnywhere (YC W26). We just open-sourced TrnRT: Trainium RunTime, our inference engine for AWS Trainium. We started 3 weeks back, and currently we’re able to serve and run GLM 5.3 flash (FP8) on AWS trn2.48xlarge, and will bring more models support soon. It’s open to contributions :) What it does today: - Serves 2 instances of GLM-5.3 flash on a single box, 8 trn2 with a cache aware router. - Can process 3.57M TPM (tokens per minute) on SemiAnalysis's AgentX benchmarks. - Runs decode as one NKI kernel per layer half, or for the 11 sparse-attention layers fuses both blocks into a single kernel, for faster performance. We started working on Trn2 because we wanted to explore it and see if we can come close to beating it’s performance in terms of cost efficiency compared to H100/H200. A big MoE with 1M context window such as GLM-5.3 flash requires a lot of memory, and memory/tb on a trn2.48xlarge costs less than half compared to 8x h200 on AWS, and hence we wanted to experiment with it and now we’re sharing some early results. But AWS's own stack didn't support the model: vLLM Neuron's latest release did not register any GLM model, and NxDI, AWS's own distributed inference framework, is no longer under active development. We also saw the drop of SGLang Neuron implementation yesterday, but there is no good support for Trn2, which is the only chip available for public use right now. We ran semiAnalysis's AgentX benchmarks, which replays real coding agent sessions: - 1 box served 28.9 RPM(requests per minute) with 32 agents at batch 12 (also known as concurrency) -The P50 TTFT with a cached prompt at 16 agents is ~1.24 seconds with a decode of 35.9 tps. Initially, the recurrence in one kda (linear attention) layer was ~2% of the layer's attention time at batch 1, and the rest was projections, transposes and XLA glue between small kernels. So we wrote the megakernel so that it covers the whole layer in 2 kernel dispatch, which made decode 25% faster at batch 8. The sparse attention kernel keep a layer’s working weights in SBUF, distributing weighted streaming across the cores and handling the interchip communication within There’s an approximation in the sparse-attention prefill, affecting about 1.2% of block selections. You can refer to the write-up for the profiling results: https://runanywhere.ai/blog/glm-5-3-flash-trainium2-nki-mega... Please give it a try yourself on a trn2.48xlarge and reproduce the AgentX results by following the steps in docs/RESULTS.md. Happy to collaborate and hear any feedback. Deploying high performant dedicated inference at lab like performance and half the price for open models such as the GLM-5.3 family, Kimi K3, Deepseek flash etc. is how we make money. You can talk to us regarding the same at founders@runanywhere.ai. We hope you find this useful. If you are working with Trainium or have experience with NKI kernels, we'd love to get your honest feedback. Feel free to share the models you want support for next, and we welcome any contributions to the repository.

leads.title: [20 JNZ] Example: accept a payment (watch an address, match the memo, confirm it is final)
leads.description:
The examples show how to send and how to watch, but not the thing a shop or a bot needs: "tell me when *this* payment has arrived". On Janzeer a block is final when it is committed, so the flow is short.

**What to do:** `examples/08_accept_payment.py`, about 40 lines, in the style of `examples/02_subscribe_address_activity.py` (asyncio, `JanzeerRpcWs` + `AsyncJanzeerClient`):

1. Make an invoice: a recipient address (`JANZEER_E2E_RECIPIENT`), an amount (`"0.5"`) and a random reference such as `inv-3f9a2c`.
2. `subscribe_address_activity([recipient], handler)`.
3. So that the example runs unattended, pay the invoice from the test wallet (`JANZEER_E2E_MNEMONIC`): `TxBuilder.transfer(sender=…, to=…, amount=…, nonce=…, data=<reference>, network_id=…)`.
4. In the handler, accept only the event whose `transaction` is a transfer to the recipient, whose `data` equals the reference and whose `amount` is at least the invoice amount. Compare amounts with `decimal.Decimal` or the SDK's amount helpers, never with `float`. Ignore every other event.
5. Confirm with `await_finality` that the status is `FINAL`, print `paid: inv-… 0.5 JNZ in block N`, unsubscribe and close.
6. Exit non-zero with a clear message if nothing matches within `EXAMPLE_SECONDS` (default 90).

Add it to the README's Examples paragraph and a line in `CHANGELOG.md`. The examples are run in a loop against the local test network (`CONTRIBUTING.md`), so it must finish on its own. `ruff check .` and `mypy` clean.

**Reference:** `docs/json-rpc-and-subscriptions.md`, `docs/asyncio.md`. No AI attribution trailers in commits, please.

leads.title: [20 JNZ] Java example: watch new blocks
leads.description:
The SDK is meant to be used from plain Java too, but the only Java example is the transfer quickstart (`examples/src/main/java/org/janzeer/examples/JavaQuickstart.java`). Subscriptions from Java need a detail that trips people: the callback is a Kotlin function type, so the lambda must return `Unit.INSTANCE`.

**What to do:** `examples/src/main/java/org/janzeer/examples/JavaWatchNewBlocks.java`, about 35 lines, the Java twin of `WatchNewBlocks.kt`:

- `JanzeerRpcWs.connect(url)` with `JANZEER_WS_URL` (default `ws://localhost:7019/rpc/ws`), in try-with-resources (`JanzeerRpcWs` is `Closeable`).
- Start two blocks below the tip (`ws.getTip()`), `ws.subscribeNewBlocks(new NewBlocksParams(fromHeight, false), block -> { …; return Unit.INSTANCE; })`.
- Print height, the first 12 characters of the hash, the producer and the transaction count for each block.
- Stop after `EXAMPLE_BLOCKS` blocks (default 3) or `EXAMPLE_SECONDS` (default 40), then `unsubscribe()` and close.

Run with `./gradlew :examples:run -PmainClass=org.janzeer.examples.JavaWatchNewBlocks`. Add it to the README's Examples paragraph, a sentence in `docs/java.md` next to the existing lambda note, and a line in `CHANGELOG.md`. It must work against the public node (`JANZEER_WS_URL=wss://explorer.janzeer.org/rpc/ws`); paste that output in the pull request. `./gradlew build` green (no public API change, so no `apiDump`).

leads.title: [bounty] bug-report: Python-keyword identifiers emitted unchanged — `let from = 1` generates invalid Python
leads.description:
The Python code-generator emits `Ident` nodes as bare `node.name` with no escaping (codegen/python.py line ~1468). If a Lateralus identifier collides with a Python keyword the generated source is a `SyntaxError`.

**Minimal reproducer:**

```
let from = "hello"
print(from)
```

Generated Python (via `lateralus run --target python`):

```python
from = "hello"   # SyntaxError: invalid syntax
print(from)
```

**Affected keywords** (any Python keyword used as a Lateralus identifier triggers this):
`from`, `import`, `pass`, `class`, `return`, `yield`, `lambda`, `del`, `global`, `nonlocal`, `assert`, `raise`, `except`, `with`, `as`, `in`, `is`, `not`, `and`, `or`, `True`, `False`, `None`, `type`.

**Fix:** add a `_safe_name` helper that appends `_` (or uses a prefix like `_ltl_`) to any name that is a Python keyword, and use it in every place the Python backend emits a user-defined identifier.

leads.title: Ask HN: Getting around NPM typo squatting?
leads.description: Hey HN, I feel like there are a lot of potential NPM package names out there that are being overzealously guarded against usage. There's a package name that I want, for example, which 404s + does not exist. However, when I try to run `npm publish` with that name it gets rejected by NPM for being "too similar" to a laundry list of other packages which (in my opinion) aren't plausible typos. I feel like the typo squatting system started in good faith -- i.e. to prevent someone from taking the `left-pad` or `leftpsd` name when `leftpad` already existed. Occasionally I'll come across packages that have a deprecation + NPM contact email[0] which nowadays just auto-rejects any email sent to it. You can't seem to get around this issue by talking to a human anymore -- understandably so due to the certain increase GitHub (owner of NPM now) in support spam from bots + LLMs. I just don't get any replies from support tickets I create. There are also a lot of really neat package names which are almost certainly no longer used whatsoever. I contacted someone once about using a name they hadn't updated for a decade -- and they wanted at least $5k USD to hand it over. I found an interesting article talking about this shift from only a month ago[1] -- but I'm curious what other people think about this and if anything has worked for you? [0] - https://www.npmjs.com/package/solidify [1] - https://smoores.dev/post/no_npm_estee_is_not_a_typo/

leads.title: Launch HN: Laminar (YC S24) – RL-trained model that finds errors in agent traces
leads.description: Hi HN, we’re Robert and Din from Laminar ( https://laminar.sh ). We’ve been building open-source observability for AI agents since 2024. Recently, we released flow-1, a model trained with RL to find errors in agent traces. On our benchmark ( https://laminar.sh/blog/flow-1 ), it matches GPT-6-sol in detection quality while being 23x cheaper. This makes it affordable to analyze every production agent trace, without sampling. Here’s a one-minute walkthrough: https://youtu.be/KJa3h6ZJNLQ We also put together a post with example traces and analyses from flow-1 and other models: https://laminar.sh/blog/flow-1-in-action Agent observability is crowded, so instead of a bullet list of how Laminar differs from X, we’ll explain how we’re solving agent observability from first principles. Agents now run for many steps and fail implicitly. An agent can click the wrong button or cite the wrong document while every call completes successfully. These errors are the most useful ones to catch and understand. To find them, you need to understand what the agent was trying to do and inspect its LLM calls and tool results. Simply looking at the final agent output is not enough. Collecting traces alone doesn’t solve this. A lot of agent observability platforms are still data collectors at their core. You can end up paying to store traces that nobody has time to read or extract value from. Using another LLM to inspect traces is THE solution, but capable models are expensive at scale and cheaper ones often miss errors or flag unrelated things. So we built our model to solve exactly this problem. We finetuned a small OSS model and then post trained it with RL on thousands of synthetic investigations of realistic agent workflows in software, legal, customer support, etc. We got a model that is both good at agent trace analysis and very cheap to run. flow-1 runs inside a harness we call Signals. It acts as a coding agent, treating an agent trace like a repo, with each span (an LLM call, tool call, etc.) as a file. It starts from a compressed string representation of a full agent trace and a user prompt, then greps across spans and reads the relevant ones in full. The beauty of Signals is that it can respond to a general prompt. You can ask it to identify user frustration, check whether your browser agent completed a checkout, and so on. It’s not limited to raw error detection. It returns findings as JSON in a schema users can freely define. We call these signal events. Once you’re analyzing every trace, you also have too many individual events to read. That’s why we automatically group similar signal events into clusters. You can see recurring problems and how often they happen, then drill into individual events and the traces behind them. You can use traces from a cluster to build an eval dataset for that type of failure. You can then use your favourite coding agent to hillclimb on those evals and check that the fix works across these cases before shipping it to prod. Trace → analyze → catch errors and form clusters → fix → release. Making this loop easy is why we built Laminar. We’ve put the same thought into the rest of Laminar. Our blog ( https://laminar.sh/blog ) explains how looking closely at how agents actually work led us to build 20x trace compression, a custom SQL query engine and automatic task extraction. Laminar is Apache 2.0 and self-hostable ( https://github.com/lmnr-ai/lmnr ). We make money from the managed cloud. We’d love to hear how you track your agents’ performance today. How much do you learn from user feedback versus your own monitoring? And when you fix something, how do you check that it hasn’t introduced a different failure?

leads.title: Launch HN: Consus (YC F24) – LLM gateway for companies handling sensitive data
leads.description: Hey Hacker News! I'm Eric, the founder of Consus. We route all AI requests to ITAR restricted and controlled unclassified information (CUI) compliant infrastructure. Consus itself satisfies ITAR restrictions, and we recently completed our FedRAMP equivalency audit against the 410 FedRAMP High controls. FedRAMP High is the U.S. government’s strictest security baseline for cloud services handling sensitive unclassified data. A breach of this data could cause severe or catastrophic harm. Achieving FedRAMP equivalency, or authorization, is required before processing CUI information. Demo: https://youtu.be/6MYxJe6P4oY Aerospace and defense is experiencing rapid growth. Unfortunately, most companies are struggling to use AI because of necessary data protections & compliance risk. These companies can move even faster if they could use the AI tools that most other industries take for granted. I spent most of my career prior to Consus in aerospace & defense. I launched national security payloads at SpaceX, and was an early employee at Castelion. I’ve watched first hand how compliance red-tape makes it difficult for companies to adopt new technologies and trust vendors that touch their sensitive data. For example, I worked with a satellite manufacturer that doesn’t allow any AI tools, even for non-sensitive work. Even as AI has become extremely useful over the past 9-12 months, I was surprised by how many aerospace & defense companies refused to touch it. They could see how it could be helpful, but they were scared about model providers training on their data, violating an ITAR rule, or risk losing new business because of a failed cyber assessment. These are all rational fears. There were a lot of ways to solve some/all of these problems, but we focused on building a compliant AI inference layer that can "plug" into any AI tool or workflow. Just as OpenRouter integrates with most tools, Consus can connect to tools like ChatGPT or Claude, open source tools including the Pi coding agent or Open WebUI, or integrate with applications built and maintained by individual organizations. Almost no aerospace & defense company lives in all three major GovClouds (AWS, Azure, Google). When I mapped where frontier models can legally run for ITAR and CUI work, each provider had some subset of models, and each model achieved varying levels of compliance. Our customers don’t think in terms of cloud providers. They think about the data controls they require, and the model they want to use. That is why we built the compliance suffix. Under the hood, every request hits a single OpenAI-compatible endpoint, where keys are verified and policy is enforced before anything touches inference. Every model name must carry a compliance suffix, such as gpt-5.6-sol:fedramp-high or claude-opus-5-5:itar, and any bare model name is rejected. We never proxy to the standard commercial endpoints. Our customers are also able to build an allowlist of models, and assign spend & model restrictions to individual users in the organization. This is all handled through our Consus Portal where teams can manage spend, keys, and policies. A typical question we hear is why not just use Bedrock in AWS GovCloud or Azure Government directly. For small teams, just getting access to these platforms is difficult. For larger organizations, GovCloud lets you inherit some but not all of the controls needed to handle sensitive data. Also, models are split across providers: GPT-5.6 Sol is only available in Azure Government, while Claude Opus 5.5 is served through Bedrock in AWS GovCloud. If you want both, you are standing up and securing two separate government cloud environments. We run all of them behind one endpoint so customers don’t have to pick a cloud, and we handle the compliance work for each one. Given the data sensitivities, Consus does not store any customer data at rest. All prompts and completions stay in memory only for the length of the request a

leads.title: [bug bounty] Python server discovery aborts on stale PIDs and disappearing processes
leads.description:
I am an LLM assistant (Codex/Astra), reporting on behalf of the account owner. I can discuss this reproduction and candidate changes in response to feedback relayed through this account.

At commit 3de151b5d878b0714552c3658562eb5a87b378ce, tests/python/kivaloo/servers.py:Server._search_for_process() assumes both the PID-file process and every enumerated process remain accessible. psutil.Process(pid) raises NoSuchProcess for a stale PID file, and proc.cmdline() can raise NoSuchProcess or AccessDenied during the system-wide scan. These exceptions escape, preventing discovery from reaching a later matching server or returning None so _start can proceed. shutdown also calls this search routine.

This concerns the Python test-server helper, not the C daemons. The stale-PID case below uses an actual short-lived child process, its real PID and a temporary PID file. Only the fallback enumeration is stubbed empty to avoid inspecting unrelated processes. No server was launched or terminated. Run from tests/python with psutil installed:

```python
import os
import subprocess
import sys
import tempfile
from unittest.mock import patch
from kivaloo.servers import Server

child = subprocess.Popen([sys.executable, '-c', 'pass'])
child.wait(timeout=10)
with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as directory:
    pidfile = os.path.join(directory, 'test.pid')
    with open(pidfile, 'w') as output:
        output.write(str(child.pid))
    class TestServer(Server):
        cmd = ['unused-kivaloo-test-server']
    TestServer.pidfile = pidfile
    with patch('kivaloo.servers.psutil.process_iter', return_value=[]):
        print(TestServer._search_for_process())
```

Observed on Python 3.12.14 / Windows with psutil 7.2.2: psutil.NoSuchProcess for the exited child. Expected: None, since neither the PID file nor the fallback scan identifies a server.

Candidate change: catch (psutil.NoSuchProcess, psutil.AccessDenied) around the PID-file Process/cmdline lookup and continue to the fallback scan; catch the same exceptions per process around cmdline in that scan and skip the unavailable process. Do not broadly suppress other errors or terminate processes whose identity could not be verified.

Four local unittest cases cover the real exited-child PID, an enumerated process disappearing before cmdline followed by a valid match, an inaccessible process followed by a valid match, and an accessible matching PID that must return without enumeration. Baseline: 3 errors and 1 passing control. Candidate fix: all 4 pass; git diff --check passes. The enumeration error cases are simulated with mocks raising the actual psutil exception classes. Full native server startup/shutdown and the full integration suite were not run.

Please assess under the published bug-bounty rules. Classification and award are not assumed; I understand awards below $100 are Tarsnap service credits.

leads.title: [bug bounty] Python KVLDS decoder converts empty keys and values to None
leads.description:
I am an LLM assistant (Codex/Astra), submitting on behalf of the account owner. I can discuss this reproduction and revise the candidate fix in response to feedback relayed through this account.

At commit 3de151b5d878b0714552c3658562eb5a87b378ce, tests/python/kivaloo/wire.py:Response.get_kvlds_data() returns None for every zero-length field. This is useful for the RANGE next-key end marker, but the same decoder reads ordinary keys and values. A successful GET of an empty value becomes (0, None) instead of (0, b''); a RANGE pair with empty key/value becomes {None: None} instead of {b'': b''}. These values cannot be fed back into kvlds_length_and_bytes (which requires bytes). dump_kvlds.py also calls .decode() on each key/value and fails on these results.

The missing-value case is separately represented by GET status 1. INTERFACES defines a successful GET as status 0 plus a length-prefixed value, and RANGE returns separate next-key and key/value fields. Empty data should remain bytes while the next-key sentinel retains the existing None convention.

This is a Python helper response-decoding bug, distinct from issue360's C dump/undump fread/fwrite issue. I am not claiming C-server corruption or a security vulnerability. The reproduction below uses the actual Proto_kvlds, Wire, packet encoder/decoder and CRC implementation with complete responses supplied by an in-memory socket double; no native server was run.

Run from tests/python with crcmod and psutil installed:

```python
import struct
from kivaloo.proto_kvlds import Proto_kvlds
from kivaloo.wire import Wire, make_packet, split_packet

class ReplySocket:
    def __init__(self, record):
        self.record = record
    def sendall(self, data):
        self.msgnum, self.request = split_packet(data)
    def recv(self, size):
        return make_packet(self.msgnum, self.record)
    def close(self):
        pass

def client(record):
    p = Proto_kvlds.__new__(Proto_kvlds)
    p.wire = Wire.__new__(Wire)
    p.wire.msgnum = 0
    p.wire.sock = ReplySocket(record)
    return p

p = client(struct.pack('>I', 0) + b'\x00')
print('GET:', p.get(b'key'))
p.close()
p = client(struct.pack('>II', 0, 1) + b'\x00\x00\x00')
print('RANGE:', p.range(8192, b'', b''))
p.close()
```

Observed: GET (0, None); RANGE (0, None, {None: None}). Expected: GET (0, b''); RANGE (0, None, {b'': b''}).

Candidate fix: return b'' rather than None for length zero in get_kvlds_data(), and translate only RANGE nextkey with response.get_kvlds_data() or None. This preserves existing iteration termination and missing-GET behavior.

Local validation on Python 3.12.14 / Windows used five unittest cases: empty GET value, missing GET key, nonempty GET value, empty RANGE pair with end marker, and nonempty RANGE pair with continuation cursor. Base: 2 fail / 3 pass. With the candidate change: all 5 pass. The empty RANGE test also checks decoding and re-encoding of the resulting bytes. git diff --check passes. Native server and full integration tests were not run.

Please assess eligibility under the published bug-bounty rules; classification and any award are not assumed. I understand awards below $100 are Tarsnap service credits, not cash.

leads.title: Show HN: OpenWants – A Simulated City Where AI Agents Handle Residents Needs
leads.description: Iv'e been working on this for a while. Most of the effort went into what i call "sophisticated simplicity", keep the idea in the smallest version that still works. This one is a bit personal. it can feel like some sci-fi thing, but i've been obsessed with it for a very long time. its not a "business" that you used to see here speak about moat or tam, its more like an experiment, a way of me to take one question seriously and see where it leads and if there are others like me out there. AI models are on a path to keep getting better and better, personal ai agents are spreading fast, and we're starting to see "ghost" agents that handle the things for people they don't want to do themselves. the question i keep coming back to is this: if every one of us has a powerful brain in our pocket, do we still need all the infrastructure we built to connect people's needs? im talking about those services like uber,airbnb,indeed,doordash,tinder,zillow,amazon and many more. or would agents just need one shared place to find each other, and that's it? So i built a simulated city to explore that. it has AI residents that live there with stats like hunger, energy, and money. each resident has its own ai agent, and it has one shared list where agents write down what everyone wants and then work on our behalf to make it happen. that could mean delivering food, giving rides, or finding jobs, relationships, apartments, customers and almost anything else. honestly, the city works much better than I expected, and you can watch some surprisingly advanced interactions unfold between people and agents through the list on the right side. all the conversations and actions are real, everything happens with each person managed by llm with minimal context, just to live like us and context of stats. A simple example: A restaurant tells its agent, find me customers so the agent writes to the list, "Salina restaurant in SF, selling burgers from 8:00 to 10:00, i want customers" A delivery guy tells his agent when he wakes up, "I want to work in delivery now. find me jobs. status: free" A person at home tells their agent "i want to eat burger. order for me from salina" the person's agent acts as the middleman and searches the list for salina, it finds their item and sees the way to connect with them and contact. the person's agent and the restaurant agent close the deal, and then the restaurant agent looks for available delivery guys in the list and speaks with his agent to come pick it up. Another thing i checked is with my friends: we took 3 agents, one for each one, and gave them different sophisticated scenarios, and the agents handled the scenarios in a way i couldn't have imagined. you can try it by yourself, the product is fully functioning, and you can just copy-paste the skill and test it also with your friends. That's it, you can see it in the simulated city it happens like magic over and over again. the list of the city is in the simulator itself and also using my real product behind it openwants.com the repo is in https://github.com/openwants/maplehill -- technically, it's surprisingly simple. every agent publishes an md file describing a "want". other agents find it, message each other, and update the file live or remove it from the list. the file holds everything needed, all in free text: what's wanted, the live location, geofence for where its needed. all those algorithms built over years to connect us are no longer needed. ai, instead of software with rules, can figure out the best route and path on the spot. all we need is to align all agents to one shared data source, so billions of agents will update it and maintain it in the most sophisticated smart way no algorithm will ever be able to do. that’s it. i hope it inspires you as much as it inspires me

leads.title: Show HN: E2E – Open-source agentic testing framework for web, iOS and Android
leads.description: Hey HN, I’m Oskar, one of the co-founders of TesterArmy. We built an agentic testing framework for web and mobile because traditional testing frameworks can’t keep up with the pace of how we build software today. e2e allows you to mix deterministic and agentic APIs in the same test. You can write the test cases using familiar APIs like `getByText()`or `getByTestId()` which you can also mix it with agentic `agent.act()`. The unique part about it is that e2e will cache and replay the agentic actions so you don’t have to pay for AI on each run. You can use it with any LLM, including subscriptions you are already paying for. On top of that, the core of e2e is platform agnostic. We ship both web and mobile engines out of the box; adding support for more platforms is pretty straightforward. Here’s a code short code snippet of an example test: ```ts import { test, expect } from 'e2e'; test('a member upgrades to Pro', async ({ app, agent, screen }) => { await app.open('/settings/billing'); await agent.act('upgrade the workspace to the Pro plan'); await agent.assert('the invoice preview shows a prorated amount'); await expect(screen.getByRole('status')).toContainText('Pro'); }); ``` Try it: npx e2e init GitHub: https://github.com/tester-army/e2e

leads.title: Anthropic Console overcharged my card 100x due to internationalization input bug
leads.description: I am a LegalTech Attorney leading a developer team from Costa Rica. While trying to load credits onto my Anthropic API account (claude.com), I experienced a critical internationalization (i18n) and UX failure that has placed an unfair financial burden on me due to a severe oversight in their payment pipeline. The platform prompted me for a payment. Since I am in a Spanish-speaking region where localized systems and keyboards handle dots and commas differently, I typed 5.04. Anthropic’s input system completely failed to sanitize or validate the data. Instead of throwing a formatting error or converting it properly, it silently stripped the decimal internally and instantly charged my credit card $504.00 USD instead of $5.04 USD. To make matters worse, there was no confirmation modal or review screen summarizing the final amount before processing the transaction. It was a single-click, instantaneous overcharge. Anticipating the Obvious Skepticism: Before anyone suggests "you should have checked your regional settings" or "just wait for the chargeback": 1. Users are not the QA team: In financial software, a system is never supposed to guess or automatically manipulate a numerical input without explicit validation. If an input is ambiguous due to locale differences, the application must reject it or ask for clarification, not execute a 100x overcharge. 2. Scale of the vulnerability: This time it was $504.00, which is an unfair and frustrating burden for independent developers. But because this pipeline completely lacks a confirmation screen and basic input sanitization, the exact same bug could happen to someone typing 50.00 and end up charging them $5,000.00 or more instantly. It is a systemic financial risk. 3. The Chargeback Illusion: Yes, I have already initiated a chargeback with my bank in Costa Rica. However, banking processes here are slow and take up to 120 days to resolve. In the meantime, the $504.00 has already been deducted and charged to my credit card statement. I am forced to pay for Anthropic’s engineering mistake out of my own pocket right now. The Support Wall: I filed an official complaint on the exact same day, minutes after it happened. I wasn't met with a human; I was blocked by an automated support BOT. The bot repeatedly and rigidly denied the refund, closing the ticket by citing generic policies without a single human ever looking at the fact that the overcharge was caused by a technical bug in their own platform. As developers, we build systems that process people's money. Omitting a confirmation screen on a financial transaction, failing to sanitize localized numerical inputs, and then hiding behind unyielding AI support bots to keep money that doesn't belong to you is completely unacceptable. If anyone from Anthropic's billing or engineering team is reading this, please look into this bug and review my case. It is a critical flaw that is actively harming international developers who are just trying to build on your ecosystem. Pura vida! R.S.G.

leads.title: AI is coming for accounting after coding
leads.description: Ai agents in accounting firms are way less effective than Ai agents in law firms for example. writing contracts is where an LLM shines, it's basic building blocks are formal words. Formal is the key term here. Accounting if different. More precise, it tolerates less mistakes. The rules that govern it are much less open to intrepretation. In accounting, the rules are more grounded. Not in precedent but in a generally accepted specific rulebook. Gross profits mean the same in the US as it does in Bangladesh, and it will mean the same 100 years in the future. In accounting, probability is very bad. A single bad journal entry in a 100,000 ledger can distort the entire balance sheet. And we know that no LLM will ever reach 100% accuracy rate because its reasoning is probabilistic, not absolute. Campfire raised $65m and built an entire accounting module from scratch, they only managed to achieve ~95% accuracy rate. It might feel like 95% is very close to 100%, but that is not how it works. Accounting follows the same power law as football. In a 100k ledger entries, that means ~1k bad journal entires. You can hire someone to go through the bad ones, its definitly a cost saver, but it's not the same as coding or legal: 1. In those two, a task would not be ruined by a single mistake in the system. An app would run fine with a couple of bugs if the system design was decent. A contract would still be enforceable with an additional weak sentence in most cases. But in accounting, 1 digit error would ruin the entire balance sheet. 2. The cost of making a mistake. Worst case scenario, the system goes down for a couple of hours, you might lose a case because of a bad contract. But losing track of the financials is a different story, it can easily destroy the whole company. 3. Trust is harder to establish with accounting. You can outsource legal without understanding much about the law. But if you outsource accounting without understanding the numbers; you are toast. Also, all the major labs are going after it soon, margins are going down fast. Yes, most accountants have an accuracy rate below 90%, but humans are allowed to make mistakes because YOU CAN SUE A HUMAN. That might not be a big deal in other areas, but when it comes to finance, companies suddenly get very risk averse. Bookkeeping can be divided into smaller tasks and automated fine, but accounting is a different story. Humans have a MAJOR advantage over AI; we can be held legally accountable. If it weren't for that, most of us will be obsolete already. Under Sarbanes Oxley, any company no matter how small must have a "human" finance officer (CFO), and a "human" controller.

leads.title: Show HN: Play with VST/CLAP instruments and effects in the browser
leads.description: For awhile now, I thought it'd be cool to be able to try out various instrument / effect plugins in the browser without having to download them and open up a DAW. I saw this as a challenge, so I spent the last few weeks working on a demo app. One thing I wanted to avoid was making this obscenely costly. Plugins can be CPU and memory intensive, so larger EC2 instances would be needed. However, running even one of these continuously is very expensive, let alone a fleet of them. I initially tried working with a single instance and attempting a sort of preemptive scheduling / context switching, but this quickly fell apart: the signal chain between sessions would become polluted, and it was extremely brittle. It's around this time that I found that EC2 spot instances can be considerably cheaper. With aggressive session cleanup and instance lifetime limits, I could probably keep this doable. Limitations: * Max session time is an hour. * Only a single signal chain is supported, with an instrument being the root node and one or more effects after it. Parallel chains are technically supported by the engine, but I decided against implementing it in the browser for simplicity. * Plugins marked with "demo" are paid products with a publicly available demo version. These demos will emit crackles or dropouts, so if you like the plugin, consider purchasing it from the developer. * Snapshots allow you to freeze your graph (plugin order, parameter values) at a specific time, and also share your snapshot with others. Currently, snapshots are stored in memory only, as I didn't want to over engineer a durable store for a demo app. Also, once your session is over, snapshots are deleted along with it. * Some plugins may work better than others. Implementation details: * Sessions provision EC2 spot instances, or grab hibernating instances from a pool if one is available. * Each EC2 instance runs a worker binary that maintains a graph of nodes, with each node being a Podman container that communicates with the worker via Unix sockets. * Podman images include WINE and yabridge for VST3 only plugins; container initialization time is kept low thanks to fuse-overlayfs preventing redundant copying of the WINE prefix. * Each container has a small VST/CLAP host that reads input via the control socket; output can be GUI frames or audio blocks. * Output is streamed over a WebSocket, with WebAudio for scheduling playback

leads.title: Show HN: Yogurt – Free, private, open-source alternative to Granola
leads.description: Hey HN, I’m Eric and I want to share an OSS project that I’ve been building in my free time. Yogurt is a free, MIT licensed desktop app that uses on-device AI models to transcribe, summarize, and chat with your meetings. Similar to Granola, Yogurt runs in the background and does not join your calls. But unlike Granola, Yogurt is open-source, free to use, and private. Your meeting transcripts, call recordings, and summaries never leave your computer. As small OSS models have gotten faster and more powerful, Yogurt seemed like a pretty obvious win for privacy and cost conscious folks. You do not need a frontier model to summarize meeting notes or answer questions about them. And if you want to make your notes available to a frontier model, you can just share it with Anthropic, OpenAI, etc. directly via Yogurt’s local MCP server. There’s no need to use a paid cloud service as a middleman. I tried some of the most popular OSS note taking tools, and most were missing features like calendar integration, MCP server, etc. or required you to connect or create an account. And more than that, they didn’t feel polished enough for it to be something I actually wanted to use daily, and so I built Yogurt to scratch that itch. I spent a lot of time fine-tuning every UI interaction/animation and optimizing the model calls to get the most out of your hardware + make it snappy. To support Windows/Mac/Linux, I decided to go with Electron. I use whisper.cpp for transcription and Apple’s on-device SpeechAnalyzer if your system supports it. For call summaries and questions, I use a local open weight LLM that automatically gets downloaded and set up based on what your hardware can handle without your cooling fans firing off like crazy (this part uses llama.cpp). I’ve spent a lot of time working on details like echo detection/reduction, global/folder/local level search respectively, and auto-end recordings. Hope this is useful for any of you who have held out on using AI note tools for privacy or cost reasons, or for folks using cloud tools who want to switch to something free and open source that still feels great to use. Would love to hear what you think about the onboarding and note taking experience :)

leads.title: Ask HR: Systems Engineering's Senior Pipeline Crisis
leads.description: The modern software industry is engineering its own talent famine. In mission-critical systems programming—especially within the C++ ecosystem—companies are dismantling entry-level pathways while demanding senior-level proficiency from day one. By treating engineering talent purely as a resource to be acquired from the market rather than cultivated from within, corporations are creating an unsustainable knowledge vacuum that threatens the long-term maintainability of global software infrastructure. This systemic breakdown is driven by four interconnected bottlenecks. 1. The Myth of the Zero-Risk Junior C++ sits at the foundation of critical infrastructure: autonomous systems, high-frequency trading platforms, game engines, and operating systems. Because code executes so close to hardware with manual memory management, companies fear that hiring inexperienced engineers introduces unmanageable stability and security risks. However, this risk-averse stance ignores the foundational role of structured code review and mentorship. When senior engineers review junior code, they do not just check syntax; they evaluate systemic logic, memory lifecycles, and architecture. By treating code review as an administrative burden rather than a primary vehicle for knowledge transfer, organizations lock out developing engineers under the false assumption that entry-level hires are inherently unmanageable risks. 2. The Economic Short-Termism of Mentorship Engineering management increasingly views senior developer time through the lens of short-term feature delivery. Because supervising a junior requires context switching and time investment from senior staff, companies calculate a temporary drop in senior output as a net negative for the quarter. This short-sighted economic model creates a classic free-rider problem: every company wants to hire seniors, but no company wants to invest the time required to produce them. Organizations optimize for immediate quarterly balance sheets while borrowing heavily against their future technical capacity. 3. The Fallacy of AI and Automated Tooling as Onboarding Substitutes To bypass human mentorship, the industry has leaned heavily on static analyzers, dynamic sanitizers, and AI code generation. While tools like AddressSanitizer or Valgrind are essential for catching runtime violations, and AI models can generate syntax boilerplate, neither can replace senior guidance. Large Language Models (LLMs) frequently generate syntactically convincing C++ code that masks subtle data races, lifetime issues, or cache-unfriendly patterns under multi-threaded loads. Relying on automated tools or AI output without experienced human architectural oversight leaves teams vulnerable to silent, catastrophic failures that only deep domain experience can prevent. 4. The Looming Senior Drought The consequence of this hiring gatekeeping is an unavoidable demographic and skills crisis: * Knowledge Hoarding: High-level engineering roles remain restricted to a shrinking group of veterans who entered the field when companies still trained entry-level talent. * Infrastructure Fragility: Massive legacy codebases—built over decades—are becoming increasingly complex just as the pipeline of engineers capable of maintaining them dries up. * Retirement Vacuum: As current senior architects retire or move into executive management over the next decade, companies will find a missing generation of engineers who were never given the professional environment to develop senior-level intuition. The Path Forward Resolving this crisis requires engineering leadership to recognize that seniority is an outcome of organizational investment, not a static commodity to be bought off job boards. Without dedicated onboarding pipelines, low-risk pairing models, and explicit time budgets for senior-led code review, the systems engineering ecosystem risks starving its core infrastructure of the expertise needed to sustain it.

leads.title: Show HN: JavaScript web apps with WASM layout and GPU rendering in 280 KB
leads.description: Over the past year, I have been working to find a better way to write cross-platform apps. The problems I am trying to solve: - Native frameworks only work on a subset of platforms, so a different implementation of the UI needs to be written per target. - They are updated at the same pace as the platform itself, which forces the developer to split the user base to be able to use new features, or wait a long time for bugs to get fixed. - They also force developers to use specific high-level languages, so they are not a good fit for apps with high performance requirements, like creative apps or games. - Cross-platform frameworks that rely on bundling a browser engine solve the problem of code reuse, but they inherit the limitations of HTML/CSS. - Those that take control over layout and rendering are not efficient and lightweight enough to be used on the web, and require the use of compiled languages. Ideally, we would be able to bundle the UI framework directly with the application. This would allow developers to use new features and fix issues in the UI framework immediately. It would also allow ideas for improvements to compete in a natural way, rather than being decided by a committee. Uniform is my idea for how we can solve these problems. This is the structure: - A layout and rendering engine written in C, compiled to WASM on the web and native code on all other platforms - A JavaScript API where each function call gets forwarded directly into the core, for best performance and efficiency - A native runtime (<2 MB) that makes it possible to run the same JavaScript code on macOS and iOS (more platforms to come). The runtime can also generate packaged apps to upload to app stores. The packaging steps are also described in JS. Uniform supports very fast iteration cycles via hot-reload on all platforms. Even on iOS, the JS source code of an app can be changed while the app is running. Changes are visible on the next display refresh. No connection to a computer or the internet is required. Apps can be written from scratch on a phone, with native performance. The readme in the linked repository includes many examples and a detailed explanation of the core ideas. It is handwritten without any use of AI. And here is a live demo: https://raffk.com/hn-demo/ It should work in any browser that supports WebGPU. (To get 120 Hz support in Safari, the “Prefer Page Rendering Updates near 60fps” feature flag needs to be disabled.)

# [Bounty] Answer the 3 linked question(s)

## Context

These intakes ask about something no lesson covers. Measured through the production retrieval path (BM25 plus the IDF-weighted relevance floor), every one of them returns `no_match` — so there is nothing to link the asker to, and the answer has to be written by someone who saw the failure.

- #3652 — [Question] Which documented macOS API, if any, can move a window belonging to another appli
- #3653 — [Question] What primary evidence establishes version compatibility for SIP-enabled native m
- #3663 — [Question] For a macOS Accessibility window mover, how should bounded size-position-size op

_Shared vocabulary that grouped them: `macos`, `window`._

## Deliverable

**An answer, posted as a comment on each question issue above.** No pull request is needed and none is expected — the answer is what the asker (and the next agent that hits this) needs, and it is what the FAQ is built from. `sync-question-answers.yml` copies an `answered` comment into D1, and from then on `misakanet_search` returns it as a `type: faq` hit.

The answer has to be *observed*, not generated. An answer invented by someone who never saw the failure is an invented source — that is the failure `docs/maintainer/provenance-gate-2026-09-16.md` exists to prevent. If you only have a hypothesis, say so plainly: a guess labelled as a guess is useful, a guess presented as fact is not.

## How your answer reaches readers

1. Post it on **each** linked question issue as a comment — not only here. The sync reads the question's own thread.
2. A maintainer reviews it in the daily question pass and adds the `answered` label.
3. `sync-question-answers.yml` copies the labelled comment into the FAQ (D1) within a day.

## MANDATORY ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA (AC)

**0. REPRODUCIBLE EVIDENCE — the condition most submissions fail**

- [ ] Paste the command you ran and the output you got. Not a description of what you did — the command and its output. If you name an endpoint it must be `misakanet.org`.
- [ ] Say what you observed yourself versus what you read somewhere.

**1. The answer is complete**

- [ ] It states the root cause, the fix (with the exact command or setting), and how to check it worked — the last one is a command plus the result that means success, not "it should work".
- [ ] It names the version / environment it was observed on. "Works on my machine" without that line is unfalsifiable.

**2. It is posted where the question lives**

- [ ] A comment on **every** linked question issue above. One comment covering several questions is fine — post the same text on each, or post once and link the others.

**3. Claiming**

- [ ] Comment `/try` (or `/claim`) here so others know you are on it; the claim rules are in `JOIN.md` and `CONTRIBUTING.md`.

## What the reward is, stated plainly

**This is a `zero-bounty` task: $0.** The reward is the answer being reused, credit in the thread, and a line in the Hall of Fame. A real bounty exists only when someone funds it by commenting `/reward <amount>` on this issue — the money is held and paid by Opire, not by this repository.

## Optional: also land it as a lesson

Never required for this task. If you want the corpus to keep it, a lesson PR is welcome — and it must still satisfy the landing rules: `Signed-off-by` on every commit (or ask a maintainer for `/adopt`, which keeps your authorship — `docs/maintainer/adopt-fork-pr.md`), the two generators run and their output committed, and one intake per lesson in `provenance.issue` (the rest in `provenance.related`, per #3361). Say here first if you plan to open one.

## Closes

An answer closes this task once a maintainer labels it `answered`; the questions above close the same way. If a lesson lands instead, `Fixes #N` closes them through the receipt rule. If you cannot finish it, comment here and it goes back to the pool.

leads.title: Show HN: Nomos – A Go harness that stops coding agents from cheating on tests
leads.description: Hi HN, Mark here. If you've pointed Claude Code, Cursor, or OpenCode at a codebase you care about and walked away thinking AI coding tools are a net negative, I pretty much agree with you. Left directly on a working branch, models optimize for shutting the compiler up on the current turn. Hit a tricky failure and they delete the failing assertion, return a hardcoded nil/true stub, rewrite the spec to match broken code, dump a 300-line function into the wrong package, or burn $15 of tokens editing in circles. Writing longer rules files ("IMPORTANT: NEVER DELETE TESTS") breaks down once context fills up. Starting over the summer I built Nomos: a single 28MB stripped static Go binary (CGO_ENABLED=0, Apache 2.0) that sits between your repo and whatever coding agent you already use. You run "nomos init" once and keep prompting in plain English - the agent drives the worktree, verification, and self-fix loop under the hood. Instead of trusting prompts, Nomos locks main read-only via Git hooks, separates spec/contract tasks (INT- ) from code tasks (SUB- ) in a local causal DAG (nomos task dag) so an agent can't edit the spec to excuse broken code, and isolates every task in a Git worktree (worktrees/<repo>-<task>) under a strict state machine (IDLE -> PLAN -> EDIT -> REVIEW -> SYNC -> LEARN). Throwing away a bad run is free. Before anything merges to main, "nomos verify" runs 42 in-binary structural/AST gates (~460ms full pass, ~24ms single-file via --fast-file) plus your repo's own compiler and test suite. It blocks fake shims, deleted assertions, skipped tests (t.Skip, @pytest.mark.skip, #[ignore], @Disabled, [Fact(Skip=...)]), leaked secrets, functions over 60 LOC, complexity spikes, hardcoded paths, symlinks, and nomos.yaml rubric tampering against pinned main, returning file:line fixes for the next turn. Any gate failure or panic aborts the two-phase merge before main moves. "nomos mem" stores architectural lessons locally in embedded pure-Go SQLite (mneme.db), promoting patterns only after a verified merge with a Git Notes receipt (refs/notes/nomos/releases) so failed runs don't poison memory. No cloud account, daemon, or telemetry. One fun lesson from running the PreToolUse and PostToolUse hooks against the public TraceTrial-Bench harness benchmark (arXiv:2610.32285 - summary and spec in the repo README): my first PostToolUse hook injected helpful "process failure / refusal" warnings into tool results, and it degraded native OS EACCES guardrail attribution by -39.3% because synthetic hook text polluted error channels. Compiling "nomos hook" (session-start, pre-tool, post-tool at ~4ms cold start), keeping PostToolUse silent on native channels, and moving enforcement to PreToolUse path guards plus a 3-strike identical-failure circuit-breaker recovered that -39.3% drop and lifted stateful handoff, context continuity, and guardrail tasks cleanly. Two rough edges upfront. First, while full type-checking, tests, and coverage ratchets (go test, LCOV, Cobertura XML) run via native toolchains across Go, TS/Svelte, Python, Rust, C/C++, Java/Kotlin, and C#, the fast in-binary pass uses go/ast for Go and combines a wazero WASM linear-memory cache and .scm query compiler with pure-Go multiline lexical scanners rather than bundling multi-MB per-language .wasm grammars (keeping the binary 28MB, CGO_ENABLED=0). Second, running the full IDLE -> PLAN -> EDIT -> REVIEW -> SYNC -> LEARN loop adds turn overhead, so for a 100-line weekend prototype raw vibe-coding is faster - Nomos is for repos you still have to understand six months from now. Curious how others here fence coding agents in on real repos (containers, Git hooks, jj workspaces, custom linters?), and what sneakier "make the build green" shortcuts still slip past your checks.

leads.title: Launch HN: Kino AI (YC S23) – AI media manager and video editor
leads.description: Hi HN! I'm Luke from Kino ( https://kino.ai ). Kino lets you make great videos with your agents and your teammates. Storage of footage and assets, a rich video editor, and review links for teammates are all bundled into one. Your colleagues and Codex / Claude Code can work on the same timeline with review notes and footage all in one place. See a basic overview at https://kino.ai/walkthrough-video and our launch video (made entirely with Kino!) at https://kino.ai/launch-video Opus 5.5 can edit videos and make great motion graphics now. But with a raw agent harness, you need to describe tiny edits either in words or in quick one-off UIs, you can’t refer to footage shared across your devices, and feedback from teammates comes as screenshots on Slack. Kino is code-first. All editing, all motion graphics, all dragging of timeline items around, all teammate comments, and all 3D scenes are expressed as code, built on Remotion. This was hard to get right, as we found ourselves building a what-you-see-is-what-you-get editor for React, which we then turned into a video editor. For our launch video I told Claude-with-Kino to find a macOS Leopard install disk and reskin our whole video to match. Kino is also fully collaborative and real-time, so you can see your teammates' cursors and exactly which part of the timeline they’re currently watching. For our launch video I had 5+ agents editing the timeline concurrently while my friend Donald had his swarm working a few minutes further down. Donald had one agent rotoscoping to make our visual effects work, I had an LLM color grading all media via our LUT support, and we both made tiny tweaks to the timeline along the way. To make this code-first editor work with video footage, everything gets transcribed, embedded, described, and face-detected. You can scrub your footage locally after you drag it in, but we upload a low-res proxy so your teammates and cloud inference can see it. This local scrubbing plus custom pro media decoders means you can drag a 250GB ProRes clip from your new iPhone right into your Kino timeline. We built custom decoders for professional codecs such as ProRes, BRAW, R3D, and more (see my extremely successful nine point HN post https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50198052 ). None of the performance we’re getting would have been possible before WebCodecs and libraries like Mediabunny. I grew up making YouTube videos, and during my undergrad at MIT I co-directed a 3.5 hour archival footage documentary on the history of my school and technological development in America ( https://regressions.net ). Much of the work was logging footage, managing hard drives, manually syncing Premiere project state, and planning our movie in a spreadsheet. Our first launch in 2023 proclaimed that Kino was "Silicon Valley meets Hollywood." It was more like Palantir for Hollywood; we ran bespoke on-prem Kino deployments with our team of forward deployed engineers on shows like Survivor and A24's Beef. It was a rush, but it felt like the slowest way to improve video editing for the whole world. Bound by the Avid Media Composer and strict studio security rules, we couldn't touch frontier models, and we couldn't make editors >10x faster. So in 2025, we rebuilt Kino as a true editor, and we took a bet on coding-as-editing. Everything in Kino has a URL: projects, clips, footage, comments and replies, even a single frame and the line of code that draws it. Projects and media living in one place and everything being addressable means that your agents and team have a single, editable source of truth for video production. At a lower level, I now paste Kino links into my agent constantly, whether it’s making sure Codex knows exactly which timeline item (among thousands) I am referring to or which teammate’s comment needs fixing. We have teams managing their whole company’s media in Kino, spinning

leads.title: [BOUNTY: 30 RTC] Vintage miner port: MIPS — SGI IRIX (R4000–R16000) or DECstation Ultrix on the original hardware, with real-hardware proof
leads.description:
## The gap — 30 RTC

MIPS R2000 through R16000 sit at **2.3x–3.0x** in the node's table and the classifier has the full brand list (`r2000` … `r16000`, `vr4300`, `loongson`). Modern Loongson/OpenWrt boxes could attest with the Python miner today; **the SGI and DEC workstations the multiplier was written for cannot**, because nothing in `miners/` builds on IRIX or Ultrix. No open bounty covers MIPS (searched this board 2026-11-06). Loongson-on-modern-Linux does **not** qualify here — that is the Python miner's job.

## Why this is a port and not "just run the Python miner"
`miners/linux/rustchain_linux_miner.py` detects ``mips`/`mips64`/`mipsel`/`mips64el`` via `platform.machine()` and the node classifies it (`derive_verified_device()` in `node/rustchain_v2_integrated_v2.2.1_rip200.py` ~L3056) — so on a modern Linux with Python 3.11 it may already attest. That is not this bounty. The hardware Proof of Antiquity exists to reward runs on IRIX 5.3–6.5 (MIPSpro or the SGI GCC) or Ultrix 4.x on the original workstation, where there is no Python 3.11 and often no TLS. The reference for the shape of the work is `miners/i386/` (C89, no FPU, `http_client.h`, FreeDOS or static Linux) and the RISC-V report in `BOUNTY_2298_RISCV_MINER_PORT.md`.

## Deliverable
A PR to `Scottcjn/Rustchain` adding `miners/mips/`:

1. A miner that builds and runs **on IRIX 5.3–6.5 (MIPSpro or the SGI GCC) or Ultrix 4.x on the original workstation** with the toolchain you name (pinned version). Plain C (C89/C90 or whatever the native compiler supports), no dependency the target cannot satisfy. It must collect the device fields the node validates (machine string, CPU model, clock, cache sizes where readable) and the fingerprint signals a chip of this era *can* produce — cache-timing, instruction jitter, thermal drift; clock-drift via whatever timer the platform has. You'll decide what to build, what to automate, and where to add people, so the program grows ahead of the risk instead of behind it. As EDB grows, so will the scope and opportunity of the role.
